title: Gothic architecture: cathedrals
subtitle: 12th-16th century
subject: art
description: From the 12th to the 16th century, Gothic cathedrals raised the stone towards the sky. Pointed arch, ribbed arches, stained glass windows: a technical revolution in the service of light.

hero.hook: How the Middle Ages made the stone fly to let God into the light.

blocks.text: Between the 12th and 16th centuries, Europe was covered with **Gothic cathedrals**. It's not just churches. These are engineering challenges: stone vessels that seem to defy gravity to let in light.
The word “Gothic” would later emerge as an insult, “art of the Goths”. However, this style combines faith, urban prosperity and technical audacity. It still dominates our city centers.

sections.title: Saint-Denis: the stone learns to become lighter

blocks.text: Gothic was born in **Île-de-France** around **1140**. The founding shock is the chorus of the [[Basilica of Saint-Denis]], carried by the [[Abbot Suger]]. Faced with dark Romanesque churches with thick walls, Suger wanted a more united, lighter, higher space.

blocks.caption: Saint-Denis: the laboratory where the Gothic learns to ride.

blocks.text: Three inventions work together: the **** pointed arch, taller and narrower; tea**ribbed vault**, which concentrates the weight on specific points; and the [[flying buttress]], an outer arc that counteracts the thrusts. Together, [[The flying buttress and the rib vault]] free the walls: large windows can be opened.

For Suger, light is not a decorative detail. According to [[The theology of light (Abbot Suger)]], colored rays help the soul to rise towards God. The walls become **stained glass**. In a society where many do not know how to read, these images tell the story of the Bible and the life of the city.
In **Chartres**, certain 13th century stained glass windows have retained such an intense blue that we still speak of “Chartres blue”: a color that has become a signature.
The cathedral is no longer a stone fortress. It becomes a cage of light.

Building a cathedral often takes more than **two centuries**. Wars, epidemics, lack of money: the project is progressing in fits and starts. **Notre-Dame of Paris** begins in **1163** and finds its form around **1345**, after about 180 years.

blocks.caption: Notre-Dame de Paris: a medieval construction site that has become a national symbol.

blocks.text: The whole town is working: stonemasons, carpenters, glassmakers. Extracting stone, transporting wood, feeding the teams: the cathedral is also an economic machine.

The style evolved: classic Gothic (Chartres, Amiens), then radiant (Sainte-Chapelle), then flamboyant, more decorative. In the 19th century, Europe rediscovered it with the **neo-Gothic**. Unfinished projects are resuming, such as **Cologne**, completed in **1880**.

blocks.text: The Gothic transformed the cathedral into a vessel of light. By freeing the walls thanks to the pointed arch and the flying buttress, the Middle Ages invented an architecture that still speaks to our cities.
